name: Pewter-Cairn
geological_features: Pewter-colored regolith covering the entire surface
Impact-scarred wastelands with minimal geological activity
Asteroid belt proximity creating ongoing bombardment risk
specific_features: Cairn-like rock formations that appear deliberately stacked
Automated beacon broadcasting on an obsolete frequency
description: Pewter-Cairn is a tiny, airless body barely large enough to pull itself into a roughly spherical shape, its surface coated in a fine pewter-grey regolith that has never been disturbed by weather or geological activity. The only topographic features of note are impact craters of various ages and a series of rock formations that bear an uncanny resemblance to deliberately stacked cairns, though no evidence of intelligent activity has been confirmed. The planet orbits at the inner edge of an asteroid belt, and fresh impacts are a regular occurrence.

The negligible gravity makes the surface feel insubstantial, as though the world might dissolve beneath one's feet if treated carelessly. The regolith is so fine and undisturbed that footprints persist indefinitely, their edges sharp and shadows deep in the airless environment. The cairn-like formations stand in a rough line across the equatorial region, each approximately three meters tall, their stones balanced with a precision that the micrometeorite bombardment should have long since disrupted.

An automated beacon, broadcasting on a frequency standard that was obsolete before human spaceflight began, was discovered during the first survey of this body. The beacon is physically unremarkable, a simple transmitter of unknown manufacture powered by a radioisotope source of extraordinary longevity. Its signal contains no information that has yielded to analysis, just a steady pulse that has been broadcasting for an estimated minimum of fifty thousand years. The cairn formations predate the beacon based on micrometeorite accumulation analysis.

Pewter-Cairn's scientific value lies entirely in its mysteries. The cairn formations and the beacon suggest visitation by an intelligence that left minimal traces, and the question of their purpose has generated more academic papers than the tiny world would seem to warrant. The planet has no commercial value, its mineral resources negligible and its position in an active bombardment zone making it hazardous for prolonged stays. Yet it continues to attract visitors, drawn by the simple, unanswerable question of who stacked the stones and why.
